vignette:
Patient: Elena, 39, City Council Member

Elena remembers the sound more vividly than the image. The wet, dull thud of a fist against flesh, followed by her mother's sharp intake of breath. She was seven, huddled at the top of the stairs, the wooden banister cold against her cheek. She could see the living room rug, a braided oval of navy and gold, and the edge of her father's work boot. She never saw his face when he hit. She only saw the boot, and the way the rug would shift under his weight. That was thirty-two years ago. She still can't stand the smell of whiskey.

She tells me she became a politician to fix things. To be the person who stepped in. On the council, she is known for her relentless work on domestic violence ordinances and funding for emergency shelters. Her colleagues praise her "passion," but they don't see the way her hands shake before a vote on the budget, or how she has to excuse herself to the bathroom when a male colleague raises his voice during a debate. The raised voice is the worst. It doesn't matter if he's angry about zoning laws or parking meters. Her throat closes. Her vision narrows to a pinpoint. She grips the edge of the conference table, feeling the polished wood, reminding herself she is not on that rug.

The nightmares started about ten years ago, after her own daughter turned seven. In the dream, she is on the stairs again, but now she is an adult. She tries to run down, to stop the boot, but her feet are glued to the carpet. Her father turns, and he has no face-just a blank, smooth expanse of skin. She wakes up gasping, her husband's hand on her arm. He's learned not to touch her first. He says her name quietly, from a distance, until her eyes focus. She hasn't told him the full truth about her childhood. He knows her father was "difficult," but she has curated a sanitized version: a loud man, a strict man, a man who drank too much. Not a man who made her mother wear turtlenecks in July.

At work, she is hypervigilant. She scans every room for exits. She sits with her back to a wall at every community meeting. She cannot tolerate being surprised. A constituent tapping her on the shoulder from behind can send her heart into a gallop for twenty minutes. She manages these moments by becoming hyper-efficient. She pulls out her phone, makes a note, schedules a follow-up. She creates order out of the chaos of her own body. But the cost is exhaustion. She describes it as a "low hum of electricity" running through her all day, every day. She sleeps poorly, eats erratically, and has stopped drinking coffee because it makes the buzzing worse.

The thing that finally brought her here was the town hall meeting last month. A man in the back row, a developer opposed to a new shelter, stood up and slammed his fist on the table. "This is a waste of taxpayer money!" he shouted. The sound was the same. The wet, dull thud. For a moment, she was seven again. She froze. The room went silent. The council president asked for her response. She couldn't speak. She just stared at the man's hand, still resting on the table. Her deputy had to answer for her.

She left the meeting early. She drove home in a fog, pulled into the garage, and sat in the dark car for an hour. She didn't cry. She just sat, replaying the thud, the rug, the boot. She thinks about that hour in the car more than she wants to. She is here because she is terrified of freezing again. She is terrified that the seven-year-old girl on the stairs is still running the show, and that one day, in a council chamber full of people, she won't be able to find her way back to the adult who is supposed to be in charge.
